notes: Starter set of notable London pubs. Coordinates are intended as gameplay targets and should be spot-checked against your map provider before production launch.

clues: Long before the docks became apartments, this riverside drinking place was associated with sailors, smugglers and river thieves.
The site has served drinkers for centuries and Samuel Pepys is among the famous names linked with it.
A replica noose hangs over the Thames outside the pub, recalling the area's grim maritime history.
The pub is The Prospect of Whitby.
Look in Wapping on the north bank of the Thames, on Wapping Wall between Shadwell Basin and the river bend towards Limehouse.
This riverside pub commemorates a ship whose passengers established Plymouth Colony in North America.
The famous vessel began part of its 1620 voyage from nearby landing steps.
The pub was formerly known as the Spread Eagle and Crown and took its present name in the 20th century.
The pub is The Mayflower.
Pin Rotherhithe on the south bank of the Thames, close to St Mary's Church and Rotherhithe Overground station.
Travellers once arrived here by horse and coach, using a courtyard surrounded by galleries.
It is the capital's last surviving galleried coaching inn and is now cared for by the National Trust.
It hides just off one of London's oldest routes south from London Bridge.
The pub is The George Inn.
Look just off Borough High Street, a short walk south of London Bridge and close to Borough Market.
According to a famous story, a landlord delayed an angry 18th-century mob with free drink until soldiers could arrive.
This old inn appears in Dickens's The Pickwick Papers and has another literary association with Bram Stoker's Dracula.
It stands beside an old toll house on the edge of one of London's largest and best-known open spaces.
The pub is The Spaniards Inn.
Pin the northern edge of Hampstead Heath on Spaniards Road, between Hampstead and Highgate.
The building occupying this site was rebuilt shortly after a catastrophe destroyed much of London in 1666.
Generations of writers and journalists have drunk here, fitting for a pub in the historic heart of London's newspaper trade.
Its entrance is tucked down a narrow passage off Fleet Street.
The pub is Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese.
Look on the north side of Fleet Street, between Fetter Lane and St Paul's Cathedral.

pubs.address: 1 Ely Court, Ely Place, London EC1N 6SJ
clues: A royal story associated with this secluded inn involves Elizabeth I and a cherry tree.
The pub's unusual historical setting was connected with the Bishops of Ely.
You reach it through tiny Ely Court, making it unusually easy to walk past.
The pub is Ye Olde Mitre.
Pin Ely Court off Ely Place, between Hatton Garden and Holborn Circus.
In the 19th century this drinking house gained a reputation for bare-knuckle prize fighting.
Its long history and tucked-away position contrast with the theatres and crowds surrounding it today.
The pub sits on tiny Rose Street, just off a famous Covent Garden pedestrian route.
The pub is The Lamb & Flag.
Look in Covent Garden, between Long Acre and the Strand and a short walk from the Piazza.
This small Soho institution became a meeting place for writers and artists including Dylan Thomas and Francis Bacon.
It developed a particularly strong French identity during the Second World War.
It is famous for serving beer in half-pints and for favouring conversation over phones and music.
The pub is The French House.
Pin Dean Street in the heart of Soho, between Oxford Street and Shaftesbury Avenue.
This Victorian pub is repeatedly drawn into stories surrounding one of London's most notorious unsolved series of murders.
Its history is closely tied to the poor and densely populated East End of the late 19th century.
It stands opposite one of London's best-known historic markets and beside Christ Church Spitalfields.
The pub is The Ten Bells.
Pin Commercial Street at the corner of Fournier Street, opposite Old Spitalfields Market.
This tiny riverside pub has literary connections stretching back to Charles Dickens.
Its modern ownership has included two very famous actors and a newspaper proprietor.
A narrow rear terrace looks directly onto the Thames.
The pub is The Grapes.
Look on Narrow Street in Limehouse, on the north bank of the Thames just west of Canary Wharf.
This remarkable pub celebrates the religious order that once gave the surrounding district its name.
Inside, mosaics, reliefs and decorative figures make it look unlike almost any ordinary London pub.
Its wedge-shaped building stands at a busy junction close to a Thames bridge and railway station.
The pub is The Blackfriar.
Pin the junction of Queen Victoria Street and New Bridge Street, immediately north of Blackfriars Bridge.
This Victorian pub is celebrated less for a famous drinker than for the remarkable survival of its historic interior.
Ornate glass, mirrors, tiles and wooden partitions divide the bar into intimate compartments.
It stands on a major east-west road between the West End and the City.
The pub is The Princess Louise.
Look on High Holborn, a short walk east of Holborn Underground station.
This small pub claims a history reaching back to the early 17th century and survived the Great Fire era.
Its decor reflects the profession practised in the imposing institution directly opposite.
One of its snug areas is appropriately known as the Wig Box.
The pub is The Seven Stars.
Pin Carey Street immediately behind the Royal Courts of Justice, between Fleet Street and Lincoln's Inn Fields.
The site is associated with a major change in London's drinking habits that began in the 17th century.
It occupies the site of London's first coffee house, opened by Pasqua Rosée.
Despite its Caribbean-sounding name, you'll find it hidden in a tiny alley in the Square Mile.
The pub is Jamaica Wine House.
Look in St Michael's Alley just off Cornhill, between Bank and Leadenhall Market.
This timber-framed survivor stood close to, but escaped, the destruction that swept through London in 1666.
Its noticeably crooked frontage hints at the age of the building.
For much of the 19th century it was run by wine merchants.
The pub is The Hoop & Grapes.
Pin Aldgate High Street near Aldgate Underground station, at the eastern edge of the City.
This pub's name and memorabilia celebrate one of Britain's most famous prime ministers.
Its interior combines British wartime memorabilia with a restaurant serving Thai food.
The exterior is famous for an extraordinary display of flowers, and at Christmas for an equally extravagant display of trees.
The pub is The Churchill Arms.
Look on Kensington Church Street, just north of Kensington High Street and south of Notting Hill Gate.
This Georgian riverside pub eventually took the name of a famous 19th-century tea clipper.
It was previously known as the Green Man and later the Union Tavern.
Its large windows look north across the Thames from a quieter stretch of historic Greenwich.
The pub is The Cutty Sark.
Pin Ballast Quay on the Thames east of Greenwich town centre and the Old Royal Naval College.
This riverside pub's name recalls the firing of cannon associated with the nearby docks and maritime activity.
Tradition links the site with a clandestine meeting involving Admiral Nelson.
From its riverside position you can look across the Thames towards the Greenwich Peninsula.
The pub is The Gun.
Look at Coldharbour on the eastern side of the Isle of Dogs, south of Canary Wharf.
A famous British composer is said to have worked on one of the country's best-known patriotic songs while staying nearby.
Writers and artists have long been associated with this very small Thames-side drinking place.
It sits on a narrow riverside lane beside the Thames Path rather than on a major road.
The pub is The Dove.
Pin Upper Mall on the north bank of the Thames, west of Hammersmith Bridge.
This pub became closely associated with London's music scene in the 2000s and with one particular singer from nearby Camden.
It was badly damaged in the 2008 Camden Market fire before reopening.
Its location puts it amid railway arches, markets and live-music venues.
The pub is The Hawley Arms.
Look on Castlehaven Road in Camden Town, just north of the Regent's Canal and Camden Market.
This huge north London pub has long been a meeting point for gig-goers.
Below it is a famous live-music venue whose name evokes the subterranean.
It occupies a prominent corner opposite one of Camden Town's Underground entrances.
The pub is The World's End.
Pin Camden High Street directly beside Camden Town Underground station.
This neighbourhood pub is known for a historic interior divided by wooden screens and unusually low openings.
Its name is shared with a royal residence well outside London.
It sits in a quieter residential pocket between Notting Hill and Kensington High Street.
The pub is The Windsor Castle.
Look on Campden Hill Road, west of Kensington Palace and south of Notting Hill Gate.
This understated backstreet pub is particularly prized by traditional beer enthusiasts.
It is associated with Harvey's, the independent Sussex brewery.
It stands on a street whose name recalls the medieval inn from which Chaucer's pilgrims set out.
The pub is The Royal Oak.
Pin Tabard Street, south of Borough Underground station and east of Borough High Street.
This compact central London pub built its reputation around cask ale rather than grand architecture or celebrity.
It has received major national recognition from real-ale campaigners.
Its narrow frontage sits on a street linking Trafalgar Square with Covent Garden.
The pub is The Harp.
Look on Chandos Place, just north-east of Charing Cross station and west of Covent Garden Piazza.
Although the present interior is largely 20th century, drinking on this site has a much longer history.
The extraordinary long bar room has high ceilings, dark timber and a row of private drinking booths.
Its deliberately archaic name fits an atmospheric building on one of central London's busiest roads.
The pub is Cittie of Yorke.
Pin High Holborn opposite the northern end of Chancery Lane, close to Chancery Lane Underground station.
